js_004: Who wrote the Korean novel Kim Jiyoung, Born 1982?
js_009: Kim Jiyoung, Born 1982 is a novel by Cho Nam-joo, published in 2016. A former current-affairs TV writer, she captured the life of Korean women with quiet precision.
js_016: Kim Jiyoung, Born 1982 came out in 2016 as part of Minumsa’s “Today’s Young Writers” series. It went on to become a million-seller.
js_018: What is the name of the novel’s protagonist?
js_023: The protagonist is Kim Jiyoung, born in 1982 — a woman with a name so ordinary she could be anyone.
js_025: What is the name of Kim Jiyoung’s husband?
js_030: Kim Jiyoung’s husband is Jung Daehyun. He works at an IT company and is portrayed as a relatively considerate husband.
js_032: As the title suggests, what year was Kim Jiyoung born?
js_037: True to the title, Kim Jiyoung was born in 1982. “Jiyoung” was also one of the most common names given to baby girls that year.
js_039: Which best describes the novel’s distinctive narrative style?
js_041: A diary the protagonist writes daily
js_044: The novel takes the form of a psychiatrist’s case report on Kim Jiyoung. Real statistics are woven into the otherwise plain, restrained narration.
js_046: What unusual symptom did Kim Jiyoung show after giving birth?
js_047: She speaks in the voices of other women
js_048: She tosses and turns, unable to sleep at night
js_049: She can no longer recognize anyone’s face
js_050: She suddenly loses all her memories
js_051: One day, Kim Jiyoung begins speaking in the voices of other women — her own mother, a deceased senior colleague. This symptom is where the story begins.
js_053: Which best describes Kim Jiyoung’s mother, Oh Misook?
js_054: She gave up her dreams to support her brothers
js_055: She finished college with the family’s full backing
js_056: She spent her career as an executive at a major firm
js_057: She raised only her daughters with special care
js_058: Her mother, Oh Misook, also had to give up her own dreams to support her brothers — showing that Kim Jiyoung’s story carries on from her mother’s generation.
js_060: What situation does Kim Jiyoung face after marriage and childbirth?
js_061: She quits her job to raise her daughter
js_063: She goes abroad to earn a new degree
js_064: She starts a business with her husband
js_065: After giving birth, Kim Jiyoung quits the job she had to become a stay-at-home mom — what’s known as a “career break.”
js_067: What best describes the setting this novel depicts?
js_069: A fictional city-state in the distant future
js_071: Court intrigue in the Joseon dynasty
js_072: The setting is the Korean society we live in today. Even in an era of fewer formal barriers, the novel traces the “invisible discrimination” that still lingers.
js_082: Cho Nam-joo (b. 1978) studied sociology at Ewha Womans University and spent a decade writing for current-affairs TV programs. That reporting experience gave the novel its dense, documentary-like realism.
js_083: Published by Minumsa in 2016, it topped one million copies sold by 2018 — the first Korean novel to become a million-seller since Shin Kyung-sook’s Please Look After Mom.
js_084: Kim Jiyoung is an ordinary woman born in 1982. Her utterly unremarkable name and résumé are exactly the device that makes this “everyone’s story.”
js_085: Her husband, Jung Daehyun, is fairly considerate — yet even he can’t fully share the weight of childcare and housework. The system tilts toward women even without a “bad husband.”
js_086: “Jiyoung” was the most common name given to baby girls born in 1982. The author chose it for her protagonist precisely to capture the universal.
js_087: The novel takes the form of a psychiatrist’s clinical notes observing Kim Jiyoung. That restrained, unemotional style only sharpens its sense of realism.
js_088: Kim Jiyoung begins speaking in the voices of other women — her mother, a college senior who has passed away. It symbolizes many women’s lives layered inside one person.
js_089: Her mother, Oh Misook, also had to give up her dreams to support her brothers — showing that Kim Jiyoung’s story continues from her mother’s generation.
js_090: After giving birth, Kim Jiyoung has nowhere to leave her child and quits her job. Losing work this way is called a “career break.”
js_091: The setting is present-day Korea. Overt discrimination has eased, but the novel uncovers the “invisible discrimination” woven into everyday life, one scene at a time.
js_104: ↻ This question will come back later
js_106: The most common name for girls born in 1982. Not one individual, but a name layered with the lives of a whole generation of women — “everyone’s story.”
js_108: Sons and grandsons treated as precious, daughters pushed to the back. Discrimination that starts before birth runs through the household like ordinary air.
js_110: Boys called first on the roll, girls blamed for wearing short skirts — small-seeming moments from school years that quietly get under the skin.
js_112: Passed over for hiring and promotion, unsettled by hidden cameras found in the women’s restroom — discrimination that has nothing to do with ability.
js_114: After childbirth, she leaves her job and takes on childcare alone. The sense of loss from losing the world that once held her up spreads into symptoms.
js_116: A slur that likens a caregiving mother to a pest. One scene condenses society’s gaze on Kim Jiyoung into a single word.
js_118: Real statistics and news clippings interrupt the confessional narration. The sense that “this isn’t fiction, this is real life” is what makes it land.
js_119: Cho Nam-joo and the social ripple effect
js_120: The third novel from Cho Nam-joo, a former current-affairs TV writer. It became a million-seller right in the middle of a fierce feminist debate.
js_123: One day, stay-at-home mom Kim Jiyoung starts speaking in other women’s voices.
js_124: Startled, her husband Jung Daehyun takes her to a psychiatrist.
js_125: The novel takes the form of this doctor’s case notes, retracing Kim Jiyoung’s life.
js_126: What happened to this seemingly ordinary woman?
js_127: Childhood — the air of son preference
js_128: Amid the special treatment given to sons and grandsons, daughters always come last.
js_129: The good things went to her younger brother first; patience was expected of the older sisters first.
js_130: Grandmother’s refrain that “men come first” runs naturally through the household.
js_131: Discrimination begins settling into the body before anyone even recognizes it as discrimination.
js_133: Roll numbers always give boys the earlier spots.
js_134: The night she’s followed by a strange boy, her father blames her skirt instead.
js_135: Dress codes and scrutiny fall harder on girls than boys.
js_136: Even doing well in school, she keeps hitting the wall of “what can a girl do.”
js_137: Young adulthood — jobs and the glass ceiling
js_138: She works hard at a small PR agency, earning recognition for her skills.
js_139: A hidden camera found in the women’s restroom leaves female staff on edge.
js_140: Women are quietly passed over for key projects and promotions.
js_141: A female team lead balancing work and childcare gives her a brief glimpse of hope.
js_143: She marries Jung Daehyun, but holiday labor at his family’s home falls entirely on her as the daughter-in-law.
js_144: After giving birth, she quits her job and takes on childcare alone.
js_145: A man at a café mocks her as a “mom-roach.”
js_146: Loss spreads through the space once held by the world that used to sustain her.
js_147: In the therapist’s office — a well-meaning observer
js_148: The doctor tries to make sense of Kim Jiyoung’s story alongside the statistics.
js_149: Yet he privately decides he’d rather hire an unmarried woman than his own pregnant staff member.
js_150: A painful ending: even a well-meaning observer repeats the same discrimination.
js_151: Kim Jiyoung’s symptoms remain a self-portrait of our society.
js_153: Drinking coffee on a park bench, Kim Jiyoung overhears a man mock her as a “mom-roach” — implying she’s living easy off her husband’s money.
js_154: Rather than one “bad person’s” insult, the scene condenses how society views caregiving labor — becoming a symbol for the whole novel.
js_155: The hidden camera in the restroom
js_156: A hidden camera is found in the women’s restroom at Kim Jiyoung’s workplace. Even the space where she earned recognition for her skills wasn’t safe for a woman.
js_157: Regardless of her achievements at work, the plain, restrained narration makes the anxiety women routinely carry all the more vivid.
js_159: The psychiatrist who came to understand Kim Jiyoung ultimately decides he’d rather hire an unmarried woman than his own pregnant counselor.
js_160: It shows that even the most empathetic observer repeats discrimination within the system — proof the problem’s root isn’t any one individual.
js_161: Has there been a moment in your own life you brushed off as “too small to matter” — but was actually discrimination?
js_162: Think about how small things — numbers, dress codes, forms of address — can pile up and press down on a person’s whole life.
js_163: Why does discrimination persist even without any “bad people” involved?
js_164: Consider what it means that even a considerate husband and an empathetic doctor can’t escape the system.
js_165: Is Kim Jiyoung’s story only a woman’s story?
js_166: Read it more broadly — through caregiving, labor, and time you never get back — and ask whose question this really becomes.
